name: Thoracic extension over foam roller

lead: You lie with a foam roller under your upper back and extend the thoracic spine over it. People use it to counter a rounded upper back and forward head carriage and to look more upright.

Proponents say it mobilizes stiff thoracic joints so the upper back can extend and the shoulders and head sit further back. No clinical study of the foam-roller drill was located; related research examines clinician-delivered thoracic manipulation, which reduced neck pain immediately in one trial.

paras: People place the roller at different points along the upper back and lean back over it for a short set, usually as part of a posture or warm-up routine alongside strengthening for the upper back.
No harms are documented in the sources reviewed. People with spinal conditions are generally referred to clinicians for exercise advice.

angle.text: Users do this mobility drill to loosen a stiff thoracic spine and counter a rounded upper back, for a more upright look. It appears in posture routines; no trials of the drill itself were found.

lead: Thoracic extension over a foam roller is a mobility drill in which a person lies back with a foam roller under the upper back and arches the thoracic spine over it. People use it in posture routines to loosen a stiff, rounded upper back so the chest opens, the shoulders sit further back and the head can stack over the torso.[1][2]

The looks payoff is a more upright frame. Forward head posture is described as an excessively kyphotic thoracic spine with the head forward of the shoulders, putting the ear ahead of the shoulder line and pushing the chin forward, and Wikipedia notes the upper-back joints can stiffen in flexion over time.[1] Mobilizing that region is meant to make standing tall easier to hold.
No trial has tested the foam-roller drill itself. Related research includes thoracic manipulation trials for neck pain and studies of sitting posture and trunk muscle activation.[1][3][4]

Foam roller thoracic mobilization, upper back extension

paras: The drill places the roller across the upper back, typically below the shoulder blades, with the person supported by the hands behind the head while extending backward over the roller. It is one of several mobility and posture exercises aimed at the thoracic spine.[2]
Postural thoracic kyphosis, according to Wikipedia, is usually linked to slouching in younger people and can often be addressed with posture re-education and strengthening exercises.[2]

Forward head posture is described as an excessively kyphotic thoracic spine and, combined with rounded shoulders, is called upper crossed syndrome. Wikipedia lists strengthening the mid and lower back, shoulder-blade retractors and deep neck flexors, and stretching tight muscles, as common exercise approaches, and describes thoracic mobilization as a way to free stiff upper-back joints.[1]
Proponents use the foam-roller version at home as a mobility step before strengthening work, with the aim of improving the visible alignment of head, shoulders and spine.

No studies found on the foam-roller drill itself. Related work includes a 2005 randomized trial of thoracic manipulation, cited by Wikipedia, that reported immediate neck-pain reduction.[1] A 2006 Spine study compared spinal-pelvic curvature and trunk muscle activation in upright and slump sitting in pain-free people, and a 2014 case-control study examined sensorimotor tests in 30 people with recurrent neck pain and 30 controls.[3][4]
